newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Meeting Netanyahu, Yeltsin says Israel ties better.
newsitem.headline: Meeting Netanyahu, Yeltsin says Israel ties better.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, greeting Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the Kremlin on Tuesday, said he expected economic and political ties between their two countries to expand significantly.

"Our countries and their leaders have finished a period of biased attitudes and have energetically moved toward each other," Yeltsin said in opening remarks in front of reporters. "This regards political, economic and trade relations."
He said that trade between the two countries -- which Israeli officials said is about $500 million annually -- "with good will on both sides could increase significantly".
On the agenda for Netanyahu, paying his first visit to Moscow since becoming prime minister nine months ago, were discussions on trade links and Russia's role in Middle East peace talks.

Under fire at home and abroad for his troop redeployment plan for the West Bank and plans to build Jewish housing in Arab East Jerusalem, the Israeli leader told Yeltsin that developing relations with Russia was a top priority.

"I can see better relations just in the fact that I, as the head of the Israeli government, am here, meeting with the very president of the country, after very complicated relations over the past 50 years," Netanyahu told a joint news conference with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov.

In Soviet times Moscow was a strong supporter of Palestinian self-rule, and was often bitterly critical of Israel. Moscow only re-established long-severed ties with Israel in 1991 for the launch of Arab-Israeli peace talks in Madrid co-sponsored by the United States and the then-Soviet Union.
During their talks on Tuesday, Netanyahu invited Yeltsin to visit Israel and he agreed, the Israeli leader said. Such a visit would be a first by a Russian leader to the Jewish state.
The late Yitzhak Rabin made the first trip by an Israeli prime minister to Moscow in 1994.
Netanyahu's government includes several prominent former Russians, including former Soviet dissident Natan Sharansky, who visited last month.
"In Israel there are about a million people from the former Soviet Union," Netanyahu said. "They represent a great potential to strengthen ties with Russia."

On Tuesday Netanyahu also met Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, who said the "two countries were moving away from general declarations to practical matters in cooperation," Interfax news agency reported.
Netanyahu's 48-hour visit, which coincides with mounting Israeli-Palestinian tension, follows a similar trip to Moscow by Palestinian President Yasser Arafat last month.
At the press conference, Netanyahu defended Israel's decision to build Jewish housing in Arab East Jerusalem and said recent disagreements with Palestinians did not doom the peace process.
He said Russia would host an upcoming round of multilateral Middle East peace talks at the end of the month.

Another issue overshadowing Netanyahu's visit concerns reports of Russian sales of advanced military technology to Iran. Netanyahu said last week he would press Russia not to help Tehran develop ballistic missiles.

Primakov on Tuesday again strongly denied that Russia was helping Iran develop such missiles, and said a nuclear reactor it was helping to build in Iran was of the type provided by the United States to South Korea.
Netanyahu travels to Russia's second city St Petersburg on Wednesday before returning to Jerusalem.
